summary.text: In physics, motion is the change in position of an object over a given time, measured with respect to a reference frame.
Everything in the universe can be considered to be in motion, and spacetime, the fabric of the universe, is expanding.
Scientists use classical mechanics for everyday speeds, relativity for high speeds or massive gravity, and quantum mechanics for subatomic behaviors.

facts.label: Milky Way speed
facts.value: About 600 km/s relative to nearby galaxies

facts.label: Hubble's law
facts.value: Distant galaxies are all moving away from Earth

facts.label: Kinematics scope
facts.value: Describes motion without considering its underlying causes

items.prompt: A sports scientist records a runner's stride length and speed over time without measuring the muscular forces pushing off the track. Which branch of physics covers this study?

options.label: Kinematics
Dynamics
Quantum mechanics
General relativity

items.explain: Kinematics describes how objects move—such as tracking distance, speed, or position—without examining the forces that cause the movement.

items.prompt: You are sitting completely still inside a high-speed train reading a book. Why does an observer standing on the train platform see you moving rapidly?

options.label: Your body experiences an active push while inside the carriage.
An object's motion is measured relative to an observer's frame of reference.
Classical physics states that all physical movement must be absolute.
Subatomic particles in your body are constantly expanding outward.

items.explain: Motion is relative to a reference frame, meaning you are at rest compared to the train around you, but moving relative to the stationary platform outside.

items.prompt: If a laboratory experiment pinpoints the exact position of a subatomic electron, what does quantum mechanics say about measuring its velocity at that exact moment?

options.label: Its velocity automatically drops to zero.
Its velocity can be calculated with complete precision at the same time.
Its velocity cannot be simultaneously determined with exact precision.
Its velocity transforms into a simple classical vector quantity.

items.explain: According to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, the position and velocity of a subatomic particle cannot be measured simultaneously with complete accuracy.

items.prompt: A puck slides across smooth ice and continues moving in a straight line at a constant speed for a long distance. Why does it keep moving like this?

options.label: No net external force has acted on it to change its state of motion.
The puck creates an internal gravitational push that pulls it forward.
The overall expansion of spacetime pushes the puck across the ice surface.
Its subatomic particles are behaving exclusively like continuous waves.

items.explain: The law of inertia states that a body in motion will stay in motion at a constant speed and direction unless an outside force acts on it.

items.prompt: While standing in your room, you feel as though you are completely motionless. Why can you not easily feel the Earth orbiting the Sun at high speed?

options.label: Human senses are completely incapable of detecting any form of speed.
Earth's oceans absorb all physical movement, keeping land completely still.
Spacetime contracts around human bodies to cancel out planetary movement.
You move along with the Earth's mass and lack an obvious external reference frame.

items.explain: Large-scale movements are hard for humans to feel because we are connected to the moving mass of the planet and lack an obvious visual frame showing our motion.

items.prompt: Astronomers observe that distant galaxies across deep space are all moving away from Earth. What universal process accounts for this observation?

options.label: The Milky Way is spinning so fast that it repels all nearby galaxies.
Spacetime itself is expanding like a stretching rubber band.
Continental drift on Earth shifts our telescopes away from distant stars.
Strong gravitational forces at the center of Earth push space outward.

items.explain: Hubble's law verified that the fabric of spacetime is expanding, causing distant astronomical objects to move away from one another.
